852.prule: Restricted two-level tone / tonal-accent system: accent 1 (toneless, level low; the majority of words) vs accent 2 (H on the word-final syllable, carried by a closed set of nominal number/gender suffixes, e.g. collective -áa, -óo, -áy, -í); function grammatical, functional load low. No established word-stress rule: the most recent specialist statement (Kießling 2024 §3.1.3) says no dedicated investigation of Alagwa stress exists and, beyond 'long vowels seem to attract stress', no conclusive statement on stress placement can be made. The only positional claim in the cited works is Kießling 2003 n.5, extended to Alagwa from the Burunge description (Kießling 1994: 25ff.) and tentative: the H of accent 2 always attracts stress; under accent 1 the penult is stressed if heavy (long vowel or diphthong), otherwise the antepenult.

On stress: Kießling 2003 n.5 asserts H attracts stress, else heavy penult else antepenult (documented only for Burunge); Kießling 2024 §3.1.3: 'No dedicated investigation has been made on stress patterns in Alagwa... long vowels seem to attract stress, no conclusive statements can be made'.

tn.quote: Las palabras mixtecas se diferencian de las palabras castellanas en que cada vocal tiene su propio tono. Por eso se llama lengua tonal. El mixteco de Xochapa tiene cuatro tonos distintos: alto, medio, casi-bajo y bajo. Estos cuatro tonos corresponden, más o menos, a las notas musicales sol, mi, re y do. ... Una palabra puede tener un tono diferente en cada vocal. ... También hay unas cuantas palabras que tienen un deslizamiento de tono, ya sea un tono que sube (ǎ), o un tono que baja (â). Casi siempre el negativo está indicado por un tono que sube.
tn.translation: Mixtec words differ from Spanish words in that each vowel has its own tone. For that reason it is called a tonal language. The Mixtec of Xochapa has four distinct tones: high, mid, near-low and low. These four tones correspond, more or less, to the musical notes sol, mi, re and do. ... A word can have a different tone on each vowel. ... There are also a few words that have a tone glide, either a tone that rises (ǎ) or a tone that falls (â). The negative is almost always indicated by a rising tone.

tn.note: Four level tones (high, mid, near-low, low), one per vowel, long vowels carry two; rise/fall glides in a few words; tense, transitivity, negation marked by tone; stress named once as penultimate.

854.heavy: Final syllable attracts stress only if 'doublement fermée': consonant + short vowel + two consonants (cvcc), or consonant + long vowel + one or two consonants (cv̄c, cv̄cc) — i.e. superheavy; word-final vowel syllables and CVC count as merely 'simplement fermée'. Penult attracts stress if 'fermée' (CVC, or a long-vowel syllable, p. 46 γ; also a final vowel lengthened by an enclitic, p. 55 n. 1). Open CV with short vowel is light (and its vowel deletes when unstressed).
854.dflt: penult (Marçais rule 2°; with short open-syllable vowels deleted the penult is normally closed; antepenult only for ressaut-derived penults, rule 3°). Souag's restatement: penultimate throughout under his cross-word syllabification.
854.prule: Maghrebi-type weight rule (Marçais: same rules as the other Maghrebi dialects): (1) stress the final syllable if it is 'doubly closed' = superheavy (CVCC, CV̄C or CV̄CC); also final in 'sursaut' forms; (2) otherwise stress the penult when the final is merely closed (CVC or final vowel) and the penult is closed (CVC or long vowel), except generally not a penult created by 'ressaut' (epenthetic re-syllabification of a CCC cluster); (3) antepenult when the closed penult arises from ressaut. Short unstressed vowels in open syllables are deleted, so non-final syllables are normally closed/long. Souag (Dellys) restates the same surface facts as 'stress consistently falls on the word's penultimate syllable' under a syllabification that makes the word-final consonant the onset of a cross-word syllable (/dʒaːbuːh/ = /dʒaː.buː.h-/), i.e. final-consonant extrasyllabicity: final CVVC/CVCC stressed = his 'penult'.
854.srule: Not mentioned in Marçais 1902, 'La constitution de la syllabe. — L'accent', pp. 45-60 (one word accent placed by rules 1°-3°, pp. 54-55; no secondary or rhythmic word stress described; 'rythme' only at phrase level, Appendice p. 59). Also not mentioned in Souag n.d./2005 (Dellys) or Benali 2017 (Algiers, Oran).

morph.rootq: Marçais 1902 pp. 54-55: 'D'une façon générale, l'accentuation en tlemcenien est soumise aux mêmes règles que dans les autres dialectes maghribins. Ce sont les suivantes: 1° L'accent est sur la dernière syllabe lorsqu'elle est doublement fermée … 2° L'accent est sur la pénultième lorsque, la dernière syllabe étant simplement fermée, cette pénultième est fermée; toutefois, il n'est généralement pas sur une pénultième qui a son origine dans un ressaut. 3° L'accent est sur l'antépénultième lorsque la pénultième fermée a son origine dans un ressaut.' The domain is the whole word including suffixes and enclitics, computed by syllable weight, with no anchoring to root or…
morph.elicq: No statement specific to how accent was observed. The only method statement is general (Marçais 1902, Introduction p. IV): 'J'ai eu pour le tout beaucoup d'informateurs. Dans l'esquisse grammaticale, la collaboration de mes anciens élèves, parfois de mes élèves m'a été d'un grand secours. J'ai contrôlé leurs dires, dans les conversations quotidiennes que la nature de mes fonctions me permet d'avoir avec de très nombreux Tlemceniens, tolbas, fonctionnaires musulmans, et aussi marchands, patrons de bains ou de cafés maures, porteurs du marché, etc.' Marçais separates word accent (pp. 54-57) from a distinct appendix 'L'accent dans la phrase' (p. 57ff), implying the word rules describe words…
morph.stmt: Maghrebi Arabic root-and-pattern morphology with inflection on both sides of the stem: subject marking is prefixal in the imperfect (n-, t-, y- 'The prefix conjugation is built directly on this form by adding the following affixes', Souag 2005 p. 158) and suffixal in the perfect (-t, -ti, -na, -ət, -u), while object, dative and possessive pronouns, feminine/plural -a/-in/-at and the negator -š are all enclitic/suffixal ('ceux des deux premières séries s'annexent aux verbes, ceux de la troisième aux noms, comme enclitiques', Marçais 1902 p. 121; '-š … se place en principe après toutes les autres enclitiques', p. 188); the article l- and negator ma precede; plurals, diminutives, causatives…

855.dq: Word stress in Algonquin is regular, but it's very complicated. (Redish & Lewis); In Anishinaabemowin, syllables that occur word finally or have long vowels are always strong. (Artuso 1998)
855.dloc: Artuso 1998 section 2.4.3 'Stress'; Redish & Lewis, section 'Algonquin Stress'
855.heavy: syllables that... have long vowels are always strong; counting long vowels (à, e, ì, and ò) as an entire foot
855.dflt: All-short words foot as iambs from the left, (ws)(ws)..., with the final syllable always strong; main stress on the head of the third-from-last foot, which for words of five syllables or fewer is the second syllable (Redish & Lewis).
855.prule: Quantity-sensitive iambic footing left-to-right: long-vowel syllables are always strong (a long vowel may form a foot on its own), short vowels alternate weak-strong, the word-final syllable is always strong; weak short vowels are often deleted. Main stress (per Redish & Lewis only, hedged 'usually') falls on the strong syllable of the third-from-last foot, other foot heads carry secondary stress.
855.srule: Secondary stress on the strong syllable of every other foot, i.e. all remaining long-vowel syllables, alternate short vowels of the L-to-R iambic parse and the always-strong final syllable (Redish & Lewis: 'Then the strong syllables of the other feet each have a secondary stress'; examples sìbi = primary sì + secondary bi, nànomidana = primary nà + secondaries mi, na). Artuso 1998 gives the strong/weak parse without grading primary vs secondary; Piggott 1978:173-174 (Maniwaki) likewise stresses all tense vowels plus even-numbered lax vowels L-to-R.

Verbs are inflected as negative with the suffix -sii" (§2.6.1); theme signs, obviation, number, mode (dubitative/preterit), imperative, noun plural/obviative/locative/possessive/diminutive and all…

856.heavy: penult whose vowel is 'non affectée du signe de brièveté', i.e. medium (unmarked) or long (macron ā-type) vowel; a breve-marked short vowel (ă-type) in the penult does not take the stress
856.dflt: unstated (source does not say where stress falls when the penult is breve-marked)
856.prule: Intensity stress ('accent tonique', a 'coup de voix' without appreciable pitch rise) falls 'en règle générale' on the penultimate syllable provided its vowel does not carry the breve (short sign). The vowel table distinguishes three quantities: unmarked = 'moyen', macron = 'long', breve = 'bref'; so medium and long penults take the stress, breve-marked short penults do not. Where stress goes when the penult is short is not stated. A separate 'accent de hauteur' (pitch rise on a monosyllable or on one or several syllables of a word, written with an acute) is described independently (= tone/pitch accent).
856.srule: Not mentioned in Calloc'h 1911, Éléments de grammaire pp. 6-7 ('Voyelles'; 'Accentuation: Accent tonique / Accent de hauteur'): the sketch places one intensity accent per word and describes no secondary, rhythmic or alternating stress (the separate 'accent de hauteur' is pitch, kept in the tone note).

morph.src: Calloc'h, J. 1911. Vocabulaire français-gbéa, précédé d'éléments de grammaire. Paris: Paul Geuthner. Grammar sketch 'Grammaire gbéa' pp. 5-33 (archive.org item vocabulairefran00calluoft; Glottolog ref 8178, the MED and only grammatical description listed for Ali). Read from the on-disk PDF as rendered (grammar pp. 6, 7-8, 11-12, 18-25, 26-32; vocabulary p. 110 s.v. jour) plus the / scan of the vocabulary.
morph.rootq: "Accent tonique. — L'accent tonique consiste dans un 'coup de voix' sans élévation sensible du ton. La syllabe qui le porte est prononcée avec plus d'intensité ou d'effort. Il se trouve en règle générale sur la pénultième non affectée du signe de brièveté." (grammaire p. 7). The rule is stated over the word's penultimate syllable and vowel quantity only; no reference to root, stem or affixes (words are described as invariable, so root = word in nearly all cases). A separate 'accent de hauteur' (acute) marks pitch.
morph.elicq: No method statement anywhere in the sketch. The only framing is the introduction: "Ce modeste travail est fait dans le dialecte des Burusè, population qui habite à environ 50 kilomètres de Bangui", and, for interrogative intonation only (not stress): "une intonation interrogative que l'on ne peut bien apprendre que de la bouche des indigènes eux-mêmes" (p. 29). The accent statement itself (p. 7) gives no indication whether it rests on isolated words or connected speech.
morph.stmt: Essentially isolating: "Le verbe, comme tous les autres mots, est invariable. En gbéa, le verbe n'a en lui-même ni personne, ni nombre, ni conjugaison, ni temps, ni mode" (p. 26) and "L'adjectif est invariable comme tous les autres mots de la langue" (p. 14); the few bound elements the sketch describes are all post-root — the optional past-tense final -a on verbs (p. 27), the 'suffixe ne' (pp. 7-8, 28), the sentence-final interrogative -a "que l'on suffixe au dernier mot de la phrase" (p. 30), and 1SG nasalization "de l'unique ou dernière voyelle" on certain nouns, on the particles ko/ha/mo and on te inside te-compound verbs (pp. 22-24) — the sole pre-root process being first-syllable…

860.dq: По ритмической организации алюторские словоформы делятся на два класса: 1) словоформы, имеющие кульминативное выделение одного слога словоформы – такие словоформы называются далее ударными; 2) словоформы, в которых отсутствует кульминативное выделение какого-либо из слогов – такие словоформы называются далее безударными.
860.dloc: Kibrik, Kodzasov & Muravyova 2000 sec. 1.2.2 (pp.181-183) + sec. 1.3.4.2 rules I-III with fn.85-86 and the 'all other wordforms unstressed' clause (pp.190-191) + sec. 1.3.4.3 (p.191); Nagayama 2010:261 sec. 2.1.3
860.heavy: двухморный (two-mora) = a syllable of any shape other than |Cə| — i.e. CV with a full vowel, CVC, and closed schwa syllables |CəC| (where speakers feel the stress on the coda consonant); одноморный (one-mora) = open syllable with schwa |Cə|, 'always unstressed' because ə cannot be lengthened. Nagayama 2010: 'the stress cannot fall on open syllables containing the vowel /ə/'.
860.dflt: 3+σ wordform with one-mora σ2: stress moves to σ1 only if σ1 is two-mora AND contains root segments (rule III: '...если же второй слог одноморный, то ударение перемещается на первый двухморный слог, если он содержит сегменты корня', schemata IIIa – – ⇒ – –́, IIIb ∪ – ⇒ ∪ –́, IIIc – ∪ ⇒ –́ ∪; fn.86 'В противном случае словоформа не получает ударения'). Disyllable with one-mora σ1: σ2 stressed and a syllable is appended (rule IIb + 1.3.4.3; fn.85: no stressed disyllables with one-mora σ2). Everything else — both σ1 and σ2 one-mora, or σ1 two-mora but purely prefixal — is an UNSTRESSED wordform: 'Все остальные словоформы, которые не подпадают под действие указанных правил, ударения не получают и являются безударными, ср. ⁻najələn ‘они его дали’, ⁻təjələn ‘я его дал’ (ударный корень {jəl}), ⁻təʕaljuljun ‘я его убаюкал’ (безударный корень {ʕaljulju}).' (p.191).
860.prule: Word stress is confined to the first two syllables and is never word-final: it falls on the 2nd syllable of wordforms with 3+ syllables and on the 1st syllable of disyllables. Only 'two-mora' syllables (any syllable other than open |Cə|) can bear stress: if σ2 of a 3+σ wordform is open-schwa, stress goes to σ1 (Nagayama 2010 rule iv; Kibrik et al. rule III); if σ1 of a disyllable is open-schwa, an epenthetic syllable is appended and stress falls on σ2 (Kibrik et al. fn.70, rule IIb; Nagayama rule iii). Stress on an open full-vowel syllable is realised by vowel lengthening, on a closed syllable by strengthening of the coda consonant. A listed class of wordforms is wholly unstressed.
860.srule: Not mentioned in Kibrik, Kodzasov & Muravyova 2000, sec. 1.2.2 and 1.3.4.1-1.3.4.3 (pp.181-183, 189-191) and sec. 1.3.7, nor in Nagayama 2010 sec. 2.1.3 (p.261); stressed wordforms are defined by culminative prominence of one syllable and all transcriptions carry a single stress mark.
860.quote: Для описания ритмики ударных словоформ удобно ввести понятия “одноморного” и “двухморного” слога. Одноморным является слог вида |Cə|, двухморным – слог любого другого вида. На ритмику ударных словоформ накладываются следующие три ограничения: 1) ударение может падать лишь на двухморный слог, одноморные слоги всегда безударны; 2) ударение может падать либо на первый, либо на второй слог словоформы (но предпочитается ударение на втором слоге); 3) ударение не бывает на последнем слоге словоформы. ... Двусложные слова имеют ударение только на первом слоге (при этом он всегда двухморный), например…

862.heavy: 'heaviness' = vowel quality, not syllable quantity: /ai/,/au/ heaviest, then /a/, then /ɒi/,/ɒu/, then /i/,/e/, then /u/,/o/, lightest /ɒ/,/ɔ/ ('A heavy vowel or diphthong attracts stress and a light vowel or diphthong repels stress')

862.prule: Predictable (non-phonemic) word stress assigned by a vowel-quality 'heaviness' (sonority/prominence) hierarchy: /ai, au/ > /a/ > /ɒi, ɒu/ > /i, e/ > /u, o/ > /ɒ, ɔ/. The syllable with the heaviest vowel in the word is stressed, at any distance from either edge (aniyopa [ʌnɪjʌʼpa], amoloki [ˈɐmɭʌkɪ]); if a polysyllable has only one kind of vowel, the last occurrence tends to take stress (unu [ʊʼnu]). One stress per phonological word; stressed vowels are longer.

A further 425 tone strings of 2+ letters carry no apostrophe, but these are almost all multi-word headwords with one tone letter per monosyllabic word (387 of 425 have exactly one word per tone letter, e.g. 'mbak nyeng (B A)', 'yag bchuux so chinn (B B C S)'), not unmarked polysyllabic words. Regex count, not hand-checked entry by entry. The dictionary front matter itself states no rule of stress placement; the placement statements ('Generalmente la última sílaba de la palabra es la acentuada. Pero también hay palabras acentuadas en la primera sílaba', sec. 2.2; 'este acento casi siempre cae en la última sílaba. 868.dq: prosodic features – there is fixed final syllable stress pattern applied to a phonological word. ... A pause is allowed between them, but no pause is allowed within them and the stress is on the final syllable of each phonological word.

868.prule: Predictable, non-contrastive word stress: iambic (right-headed) disyllabic feet built from the right edge of the phonological word; primary stress on the head of the rightmost foot = final syllable; secondary stress on the head of the second foot from the right (e.g. 4-syll cì.klɔ̄ˌ.lāŋ.sɔ́ˈ). Affixes are stressed when word-final; single clitics and nominal suffixes -po/-pe/-so are unstressed and do not shift stress; with two clitics (or suffix+clitic) the last clitic is stressed.
868.srule: Secondary stress on the head of the second binary iambic foot from the right edge, i.e. the antepenult in words of four or more syllables (ex. 2.6 cì.klɔ̄ˌ.lāŋ.sɔ́ˈ 'star'); trisyllables have one foot and no secondary stress (ex. 2.7). Stress on further feet leftward is not discussed.

Position is fixed relative to the root and morpheme class, not computable from syllable count; no weight conditioning.

870.dq: There are three accents in Greek. No Greek accent can stand farther back than the antepenult. ... An accent is called recessive when it moves back as far from the end of the word as the quantity of the ultima permits
870.heavy: ultima 'long, either by nature or by position' (long vowel/diphthong, or short vowel followed by two consonants) blocks antepenult accent — conditions the accent window, not a stress rule
870.prule: Pitch (musical) accent, not stress: one accent per word, confined to the last three syllables; position is lexical ('has to be learned by observation') within a quantity-conditioned window (a long ultima, by nature or position, bars accent on the antepenult). Dialect-specific for the North Greek group: Lesbian Aeolic generalises recessive accent (as far from the word end as the ultima's quantity permits) to all words except prepositions and conjunctions, making position predictable there; Doric is reported by ancient grammarians as 'processive' in certain form classes, but Buck judges the evidence too meager to generalise and unknown for most Doric dialects.
870.srule: Not mentioned in Smyth 1920, Accent chapter sections 149-188 (pp. 37-43), or Buck 1910 section 103 (p. 79): one pitch accent per word (compounds 'united under one accent', 869 b); the only additional word-level accent described is the enclitic-induced second acute on a proparoxytone/properispomenon host (183 c), a pitch-accent sandhi fact, not secondary stress.

871.prule: Phonemic (contrastive) expiratory word stress that replaced OA vowel/syllable quantity (AA has no vowel length). 877.dq: Farquhar 1974 p.92: 'a compound has only one main stress, whereas a phrase consisting of the same elements has at least two.'
877.dloc: Farquhar 1974 pp. 25, 29, 61, 92 (excerpt); Galarza Ballester thesis p.146 (open text); Aceto & Williams 2004 p.487 (excerpt)
877.prule: No positional word-stress rule is stated in any reachable text. Farquhar 1974 treats primary stress as a given (English-inherited) word property: it marks it with an acute in examples (/dem a-kóm/), uses it to distinguish stressed vs unstressed function-word doublets (numeral /wan/ vs article /wan/, stressed negative /kā/), notes stress-conditioned vowel raising in go/come, and states that a compound has one main stress vs a phrase at least two. The only placement statement is segment-linked: the syllable containing the palatal stop+glide (kya, gya) carries primary stress (Galarza p.146, Wikipedia citing Farquhar). Regionally, Aceto & Williams 2004 report many words with final stress where metropolitan English has initial stress (rea'lize) — a word-by-word (lexical) difference, not a rule.
